transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, they told me I had to come in, my supervisor down at the building where I clean, because of the way I've been talking lately. It's like... well, it's like my talking gets all mixed up, you see? I try to explain things, important things, like about the keys to the supply closet on the third floor, because there's a whole system to them, but then I start thinking about the jail, because the keys remind me of the jail down on 4th street and how the locks there must be so heavy, and then I have to mention the prayer rug, because I saw one in a magazine that looked just like the floor tiles in the lobby, and from there it's just a straight line to the chess pieces, the knights specifically, because of how they move in an L-shape just like the mop bucket when I go around the corners. And I try to lay it all out for them, just like that, so they understand the connections, but my supervisor and the other guys, they just stare at me and tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They say I'm not making any sense, but to me, it's all connected, the keys, the jail, the rug, the chess... but it comes out of my mouth and people just get confused and tell me I need help with my words.
How long have you been experiencing this change in your thinking and talking?

Well, if you really want to put a pin in the calendar and track it all the way back, it’s been... let me think, it’s been about two years and five months. Yes, exactly two years and five months, because I remember the season and how the floors were getting all scuffed up with the weather, requiring the heavy-duty wax. It started right after this... well, this misunderstanding we had down at the building. 

It was just a big misunderstanding, really, but it ended up with me having a brief detention. Just a brief one! They held me for a little bit because people weren't listening to how I was explaining the way things needed to be organized, and things got blown out of proportion. But ever since I got back from that detention—two years and five months ago—that’s when my supervisor says my talking really started changing. I think it's because ever since that misunderstanding, I've been trying so hard to make sure everybody understands all the pieces and how they fit together, so there aren't any more misunderstandings, you know? I have to explain the whole picture. But I guess the harder I try to explain it all, the more they say my words are changing and I'm not making sense. But the timeline, yes, it's been two years and five months since that brief detention.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds when no one else was around, that other people couldn't hear?

Well, it's... it's funny you ask about that, because yes, I do. But you have to understand, it’s not just random noises like the old pipes settling or the elevator cables clanking in the shafts, because I know all the sounds that building makes. I know every creak. No, this is... this is a voice. It's a man's voice. 

It usually happens when I'm entirely alone, like when I'm mixing the heavy-duty floor cleaner in the mop closet on the second floor, or when I'm walking past those big metal air vents in the main hallway. The vents with the heavy aluminum grates, you know the ones? The voice comes right out of there, or right out of the dark in the closet. And it's not just a whisper or a mumble, doctor. He says my name. He calls out my name, clear as a bell, and then he tells me that I ruined everything. Over and over. He says I ruined everything. 

And I always stop what I'm doing, I let go of the mop wringer, and I look around, because I swear to you on my life, it sounds exactly as real as someone standing right beside me. Like a full-grown man is standing right at my shoulder, close enough that I should be able to feel him breathing, telling me how I ruined it all. I even leave my cart and go check the stairwells, checking the heavy fire doors to see if somebody from the day shift stayed late or snuck in, because the sound is just so real, so solid in the air. But there's never anybody there. Just me and the buckets. But I hear him all the same, coming from the vents, telling me I ruined it all.
During these past two years, have you experienced any periods where you felt deeply sad, hopeless, or lost interest in things for weeks at a time?

Well, yes... yes, there are times. Whole stretches of time, actually, weeks where the days just bleed together into one long, gray shadow. It's like... well, you know those thick, heavy moving blankets we use to protect the elevator walls when the office workers are moving big metal desks? It feels like one of those is just draped right over my shoulders, soaking wet, just pressing me down into the mattress. 

On my bad days—and there have been so many of these periods over the last two years, whole weeks where the sun doesn't even seem to reach my window—I'll wake up and I'll do my morning prayer. I always try to do my morning prayer, right there by the radiator. But right after that... I just sit on the edge of the bed. I sit there on the edge of the mattress feeling so heavy and empty. It's a strange thing, doctor, to feel heavy and empty at the exact same time, like a hollowed-out iron pipe. 

I look at my work boots sitting there on the linoleum, and I just feel like there is no point cleaning myself up or going outside. No point at all. I think about the soap, I think about turning the handles on the sink, the bus ride down to the building, and it all just feels completely impossible. The dust is just going to come back, the floors are just going to get scuffed again by all those shoes, so what does it even matter? I'll just sit there on the edge of that bed for hours, staring at the dirt on my boot laces, not even turning on the radio, just completely lost in this... this deep, dark pit where nothing has any color or purpose anymore. And that feeling, that terrible heaviness, it just stays with me day after day, week after week, until I can barely remember what it feels like to actually care about anything. I just sit and sit, and the time goes by, and the emptiness just swallows up the whole room.
Do you still hear the voice or have trouble with your thoughts even during times when you are not feeling down or depressed?

Well, that’s... that’s the thing that really gets me, doctor. Because you’d think, wouldn’t you? You’d think that if the heavy blanket lifted, if that terrible, hollow feeling went away and I could actually get up and put my boots on and go to work without feeling like I was carrying the weight of the whole building... you’d think the voice would go away, too. But it doesn't. 

There have been weeks, whole stretches of time, where I feel completely... well, I wouldn't say normal, because what is normal, really? But I feel calm. I'm not trapped in that dark pit sitting on the edge of my bed, and I'm not all wound up and racing around trying to explain everything to everyone either. I'm just... steady. Just doing my job, mixing the wax, sweeping the lobbies. But even during those calm weeks—and I've kept track, doctor, I've had periods lasting a good two, three weeks, maybe more, where my mood was perfectly fine, perfectly level—I still hear him. 

I'll be walking past those heavy aluminum grates, feeling perfectly fine, and there he is. "You ruined everything." Right out of the vents. Clear as day. And it's not just the voice, either. During those exact same calm weeks, when I'm not depressed at all, I still see what the people in the building are doing. I see the way the office workers tap their coffee cups on the security desk when I walk by. Two taps, then a pause, then one tap. They do it to signal to each other about me. Or the way the security guards will adjust their radios, turning the volume knob specifically when I'm emptying the trash cans near them. They think I don't notice the signals, but I do. I see it all. And that happens even when I'm having a good week, even when I'm not sad or overly energized. For weeks at a time, the mood is fine, but the man in the vents and the signals... they just never stop.
Looking back over the entire two and a half years since this all started, would you say you felt depressed for most of that total time, or only a smaller part of it?

Well, let me think on that, doctor, because two and a half years... that’s a lot of days to look back on. You figure, in two and a half years, I’ve had to do the deep chemical strip and wax on the main lobby floors maybe five times, right? Because the building management has us do that every six months, regular as clockwork. So I try to measure the time by that, by the work schedule and the seasons. 

And when I really sit down and add it all up—all those weeks where that heavy, wet moving blanket was draped over me, where I couldn't get off the edge of the mattress and just stared at the dirt on my boot laces—it doesn't actually make up the majority of the time. It's not even half. I'd say... well, if you take all those bad stretches, the ones in the dead of winter when the building's boiler is running hot, and the ones in the summer when the big AC units are humming, and you stack them all end to end... it adds up to about seven months. Just about seven months total out of the whole two and a half years. 

So, I guess you'd say that’s a smaller part of the total time, mathematically speaking. But I have to tell you, doctor, when you're in the middle of it, when you're just sitting there in that dark pit and the dust is gathering on the floorboards and you can't bring yourself to even turn the hot water handle on the sink... a single week feels like a whole lifetime. It really does. It stretches out so long you think it's never going to end. But if I'm being exact, if I'm looking at the little pocket calendar I keep in my locker down in the basement, those heavy, hopeless periods, they've added up to about seven months during this whole illness.
